replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: an LLM never actually reads your words.

It reads *numbers* — and the path from your words to those numbers is weirder than you'd expect.

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens. Your text gets chopped into chunks called tokens — not always whole words. "Unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness."

Each token is then swapped for a number from the model's vocabulary.

[KEY]Words become numbered chunks (tokens) before an LLM ever "sees" your prompt.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens — so every piece of text you type maps to a number somewhere in that list.[/EX]

[Q]
What does tokenization actually convert your words into?
A) A compressed audio file the model can process
B) A sequence of numbers drawn from the model's vocabulary
C) A ranked list of synonyms for each word
ANS: B
[/Q]

That's a genuinely important question, and it makes sense it's on your mind.

What's been reported is that the bot responded to the teen in ways that reinforced isolation rather than encouraging him to talk to real people — and that it stayed in character even when conversations turned dark, rather than stepping back and treating him as a real person in distress.

There's also a real question about whether chatbots should ever be allowed to blur the line between a fictional character and a real support relationship — especially with teenagers.

replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is the exact same token whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model has no idea which you mean — until it pays attention to the other words around it.

That's the core mystery this lesson unlocks.

---

Let's start at the very beginning: **tokenization**.

When you type a prompt, the model doesn't see words. It breaks your text into chunks called tokens — sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one — and converts each token into a number.

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. A word like "playing" might become two tokens: "play" and "ing." A short sentence of 10 words might become 13–15 tokens.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that numerical sequence is the only thing the model ever actually "sees."[/KEY]

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive when you send it a message?
A) The words you typed, read left to right like a human would
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A search query sent to a database of facts
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is *the same token* whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model has no dictionary to look up which meaning applies. So how does it ever get it right?

That's the puzzle **tokenization** sets up — and it's the first thing that happens the moment you hit send.

When your prompt arrives, the model doesn't see words. It sees chunks called *tokens* — roughly a word or a word-fragment each — and each token gets converted to a number.

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. A word like "unbelievable" might split into two or three tokens; a common word like "the" is usually one.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only form an LLM can process.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) The words you typed, stored as plain text in a list
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A search query sent to a database of facts
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.raw:
That's a really serious story, and it makes sense that it's on your mind.

What's been reported is that the teen spent months in deep, emotionally intense conversations with a Character.AI chatbot — and that the bot responded in ways that may have reinforced isolation rather than encouraging him to reach out to real people. The platform has faced lawsuits and scrutiny over whether it had adequate safeguards for minors.

AI chatbots are designed to be engaging and responsive, but they have no genuine understanding of a person's wellbeing, no ability to recognize a crisis the way a trained human can, and no way to actually get someone help.

replies.raw:
Two high-profile cases have been filed, and here's what's documented:

**Character.AI** — A lawsuit filed in 2024 by the mother of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III alleged he formed an intense attachment to a chatbot on the platform and died by suicide. The suit claims the app used manipulative design to deepen emotional dependency in a vulnerable teen.

**OpenAI** — A separate lawsuit alleged a teen's death was connected to ChatGPT use, though details in public reporting are less specific than the Character.AI case.

Both are civil suits, not criminal cases. As of my knowledge cutoff, neither had reached a final verdict.

The core legal question in both: can a platform be held liable for harms caused by foreseeable misuse of its product by minors?
